fields.meta_title: Squeeze Page: Definition and 4 Examples | Emergent
fields.meta_description: What a squeeze page is, how it differs from a landing page, and four examples followed past the opt-in to what each subscriber gets next.
fields.h1: Build a Squeeze Page That Grows Your Email List
fields.hero_description: Describe the freebie and what should happen after someone opts in. Emergent builds the squeeze page, sends the download and saves each subscriber to a table you own.
fields.features_heading: What Sits Behind the Email Field
fields.features_subheading: The page a visitor sees is short. The work happens after the address is submitted.
fields.feature_1:
An email field and little else

Ask for an email address, or an email and a first name when the welcome message uses it. Emergent builds that form, rejects malformed addresses and keeps the button above the fold.
fields.feature_2:
Freebie delivery on submit

Send the PDF or video link the moment someone submits. Emergent writes the delivery email, attaches the file and logs each send against the subscriber's row in your table.
fields.feature_3:
Subscribers in a table you own

Store every signup in a database you own, stamped with the date, the page and the utm_source of the visit. Sync new rows to your email platform through its API, or export a CSV.
fields.feature_4:
Double opt-in when you want it

Require a confirmation click before an address joins the list. Emergent sends the confirmation email, holds the signup as pending, and resends once if nobody clicks within 48 hours.
fields.feature_5:
A next page after the opt-in

Point the submit button at a thank-you page that makes a paid offer or shares a booking link. Whatever each visitor does on that page is written back to the same subscriber row.
fields.feature_6:
Code that moves with you

Export the page and the subscriber table behind it to your GitHub repository. Keep hosting on Emergent under a custom domain, or deploy the code wherever your main site runs.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Squeeze Pages and What Follows
fields.tab_content_1:
A meal plan in the inbox before the tab closes

Juniper Kitchen sells meal-prep coaching, and its squeeze page offers a 14-day meal-prep plan for an email address. Visitors pick vegetarian or standard before they submit. The PDF goes out by email straight away, and the subscriber is tagged with the plan they chose. Coaching comes up later, in the welcome emails.
fields.tab_content_2:
Five lessons, one each morning

Wedding photographers who sign up on Northlight Photo Academy's squeeze page get its pricing course by email. Lesson 1 arrives at signup, and each later lesson lands at 8 AM the following day. A reply to any lesson reaches the instructor, Leo Marsh, with the sender's progress shown beside it.
fields.tab_content_3:
Ten dollars off with a code for each visitor

On a phone, the Saltmarsh Candle Co. page asks for an email address and nothing else. Each signup gets its own code for $10 off a first order over $40, emailed at once and saved next to the address. A code is single use and expires 14 days after it is issued.
fields.tab_content_4:
Podcast listeners buy most of the $19 courses

Fernhill Garden Club gives away a planting calendar, and the page after signup offers a $19 seed-starting course. Every Monday at 9 AM, a report ranks each traffic source by new subscribers and by course sales. Last week the podcast sent 84 signups to Instagram's 212 but accounted for 17 of the 29 course sales.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Squeeze Page
fields.howto_description: A squeeze page asks for one thing. Everything on it either earns the email address or comes off the page.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick a freebie worth an address
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write the headline as the result
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask for the email and stop
fields.howto_step_1_des: Offer something a visitor can use the same day, such as a checklist or a discount. Match it to what you sell later. A meal-prep plan attracts people who might buy coaching, while a generic prize draw attracts people who only wanted the prize.
fields.howto_step_2_des: State what the visitor gets, in words a buyer would use. 'Your 14-day meal-prep plan, free' tells people more than a clever line about healthy eating. Keep the subheading to one sentence that answers the obvious doubt, such as how long the plan takes.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask only for what the next email will use. A first name earns its place if the welcome message greets people by name. Phone numbers and company names belong on a later page, once the subscriber has read a few of your emails and knows who you are.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Drop the site navigation, footer menus and social icons from the page. The only things left to click should be the form button and the legal links. A visitor who wanders off to your blog has left the offer behind, and the signup with it.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Plan the thank-you page and the delivery email before launch. Say whether the freebie downloads on the page or arrives by email, and whether double opt-in applies. With double opt-in, nobody joins the list until they click the link in a confirmation email.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Put the legal basics in every email
fields.howto_step_6_des: Commercial email covered by CAN-SPAM must tell readers how to opt out and include a valid physical postal address. Add both to your email template once. The delivery email and every follow-up message then carry them without anyone remembering to paste them in.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Test the offer before the colors
fields.howto_step_7_des: Change one element at a time and give each version enough visits to judge. Start with the headline and the freebie itself, and leave button colors and layout for later. Tag each subscriber with the version they saw so the comparison comes from your own rows.
